title: Trees Use Hidden 'Muscles' to Straighten Themselves
summary:
Trees cannot walk or stretch, yet they can sense their own shape and adjust how they grow to stay upright. This awareness of body position is called proprioception. It was once thought to exist only in animals, but in 2012 researchers working with INRAE demonstrated that plants also possess this ability. Scientists knew plants could detect their shape, but how they turned that information into movement remained a mystery.

Plants also respond to gravity and sunlight, so researchers built an unusual test to isolate this hidden sense. Young trees were placed on a horizontal platform rotating inside a sphere lit equally from every direction. Rotation prevented a consistent signal from gravity, and the even light removed clues about which way to grow.

The work began with young poplar trees placed horizontally. As they grew, their stems curved upward. That bending depends on tension wood, a special wood that can generate pulling forces as it develops. When it forms on the upper side of a stem, it acts much like a contracting muscle, pulling the stem upward.

After about ten days, once the trees had developed a noticeable curve, researchers moved them into the rotating apparatus. Over the following weeks, the curved stems slowly straightened until they were nearly straight again.

Examining the new wood explained why. The original tension wood on the upper side stopped developing, and identical tension wood began forming on the opposite side. This new wood acted like an opposing muscle, pulling in the other direction until the forces balanced.

Scientists previously believed tension wood formed only on the upper side of stems. The discovery shows it can work on opposing sides, much like opposing muscle groups in animals. That ability could help trees recover their posture after storms or other disturbances bend them.
why_it_matters: Understanding how trees recover after being bent could help people care for forests damaged by storms. It also changes how scientists think about tension wood, which was previously believed to form only on the upper side of stems.
